questions.q: Why does this lesson describe a hybrid environment with separately governed on-prem and cloud identity policies as a real security gap?
options: Because on-premises Active Directory cannot technically support multi-factor authentication
Because a domain admin credential is still a domain admin credential regardless of which side of the boundary an attacker compromised it from
Because cloud identity providers do not support password hashing
Because Microsoft Entra Connect only works for organizations with fewer than 500 users
questions.explain: An attacker doesn't care whether a privileged credential was compromised on-prem or in the cloud — if one side is loosely controlled, that weakness undermines protection on the other side too.

questions.q: What does Microsoft Entra Connect actually do, according to this lesson?
options: It synchronizes on-prem AD accounts, group memberships, and password hashes into Microsoft Entra ID, so a user has one recognized identity
It replaces on-premises Active Directory entirely so no domain controllers are needed
It encrypts all traffic between a user's device and a cloud application
It automatically applies the AD tiering model to every account without configuration
questions.explain: Entra Connect (formerly Azure AD Connect) is the sync mechanism that keeps on-prem and cloud identity from becoming two separate, drifting systems by giving a user one identity both sides recognize.

questions.q: In Microsoft's AD tiering model, what is the hard rule between Tier 0, Tier 1, and Tier 2?
options: All three tiers share the same administrative credentials for convenience
Tier 2 workstations have higher privilege than Tier 0 domain controllers
A credential valid at one tier is never allowed to log on to a system at a more sensitive tier
Tiering only applies to cloud subscriptions, never to on-premises systems
questions.explain: The tiering model's core rule is that a lower-tier (less sensitive) credential must never be usable to log on to a higher-tier, more sensitive system, such as a domain controller.

questions.q: Why does a Privileged Access Workstation (PAW) matter even if the AD tiering rule is correctly enforced on paper?
options: A PAW is only needed for compliance paperwork, not for actual security
A PAW replaces the need for credential vaulting entirely
A PAW is required by law in every jurisdiction that uses Active Directory
If a Tier 0 credential is typed on a lower-trust, possibly compromised machine, malware on that machine can capture it regardless of how the tiering policy is written
questions.explain: Tiering policy alone can't stop credential theft at the point of entry — a PAW is a hardened, single-purpose device that removes the opportunity for malware to be present when a Tier 0 credential is typed.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is required to achieve unified hybrid segmentation, rather than separate on-prem and cloud security programs?
options: Running identity sync, hybrid Conditional Access, AD tiering, and PAWs together under one consistent policy, rather than as separate programs
Decommissioning on-premises Active Directory as soon as possible
Relying on cloud Conditional Access alone, since on-prem resources are considered out of scope for Zero Trust
Issuing every employee a separate identity for on-prem and cloud resources
questions.explain: The lesson's conclusion is that unified hybrid segmentation requires all four real mechanisms — identity sync, hybrid Conditional Access, AD tiering, and PAWs — run together under one policy, not treated as separate on-prem and cloud efforts.
